title: Three bodies
hook: the Buddha as the truth body, the bliss body and the body that appears in the world

segments.voice: Yesterday, Buddha-nature: gold under the muck, a statue wrapped in rags. Your line was covered, not lost. Who did you try it on? Day one thousand one hundred three.

A monk named Vakkali is sick in bed, and he has one wish: to see the Buddha with his own eyes one more time. Word is sent, and the Buddha comes and sits by him. Vakkali tries to get up. The Buddha tells him to lie still. And then, instead of a soft word, a sharp question: why do you want to see this foul body? Whoever sees the teaching, he says, sees me. Whoever sees me sees the teaching. That line is in the Pali texts, and later Buddhists built a whole picture of the Buddha around it. Today, the three bodies.
screen: `A SICK MONK'S WISH.` → `WHY SEE THIS BODY?` → `WHO SEES THE TEACHING SEES ME.`

segments.voice: In the Mahayana, the question of what a Buddha is grows into a three-part answer. Trikaya: three bodies. Body here doesn't only mean flesh. It's closer to a form, or a way of being present. First, the truth body, the dharmakaya. This is the Buddha as truth itself, what was seen on the night of awakening. It has no edges, no birthday and no address. When the Buddha told Vakkali that whoever sees the teaching sees him, Mahayana readers heard this body. Second, the bliss body, the sambhogakaya. This is the Buddha as the Mahayana sutras describe him in glory: radiant, teaching great bodhisattvas in pure lands, beyond ordinary sight. Some Tibetan and East Asian practices picture the Buddha this way. Third, the body that appears, the nirmanakaya. This is the Buddha who is born, walks the roads, eats rice, falls ill and dies: the life this path followed in its stories. In this picture the human life is real, and it is also the truth taking a form people could meet and follow. One image some teachers use is the moon: the moon itself, its light, and its reflection in a bowl of water. One moon, met three ways. Schools explain the three bodies differently, and the teaching in this form is Mahayana; Theravada Buddhists speak of the Buddha's life and of the teaching he left, without the three-body scheme. What the teaching does is widen an old question. Where is the Buddha now? One answer: in the teaching, for anyone who sees it. Another: in forms suited to whoever is looking. Another: in a life once lived on real roads.
screen: `THE TRUTH BODY: DHARMAKAYA.` · `THE BLISS BODY: SAMBHOGAKAYA.` · `THE BODY THAT APPEARS: NIRMANAKAYA.` · then, large: `ONE MOON, MET THREE WAYS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, if you'd like. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind someone who matters to you and isn't in the room. Notice three ways they're present anyway. First, what they stand for: the thing they taught you, which would stay true even if you never saw them again. Second, how they appear in your mind's eye, bright and particular: a laugh, a way of standing in a doorway. Third, one real moment, a place and a day when you were actually together. Rest with all three for a while. Then let them go, and come back to the breath. The bell holds the time.
Trikaya. Three bodies: the Buddha as the truth itself, as the bliss body in glory, and as the body that appears in the world. Today's word.
Your line: three bodies. Today, when you think of someone you miss, notice which of the three ways they're showing up. Tomorrow, many Buddhas, many worlds. Day one thousand one hundred three.

howItsDone: Mahayana teachers in Tibet and East Asia use the three bodies to explain how the Buddha is present: in the teaching, in visions and pure lands, and in the human life told in the Buddha's story.

fork.setup: you're the Buddha. a sick monk who loves you has begged to see you one more time, and you've come to his bedside. what do you say?
options: stay, and let him look as long as he likes
ask why he wants to see this body, and say whoever sees the teaching sees you
fork.reveal: in the Pali text the Buddha turns him from the body to the teaching. Mahayana readers later heard the truth body in that line.

original.note: Sanskrit: tri, three, and kaya, body: the three ways a Buddha is present.

trapdoor: what you thought: a statue of a Buddha with three bodies.
what it means: one Buddha, present three ways: as truth itself, in glory to bodhisattvas, and as a human life on real roads.
what a scholar hears: dharmakaya, sambhogakaya, nirmanakaya, a Mahayana scheme that some readers connect to the Pali line, whoever sees the teaching sees me.

sources.ref: Mahayanasutralamkara, on the three bodies of a Buddha

notes: Vakkali (SN 22.87) is paraphrased, not quoted: the Buddha asks why he wants to see this 'foul/putrid body' and says whoever sees the Dhamma sees him, and whoever sees him sees the Dhamma. The later part of the sutta (Vakkali's death) is left out deliberately.

The moon image (moon, light, reflection) is attributed only to 'some teachers'; confirm it is a recognized teaching image for the three bodies, or replace it (a Tibetan image is sky, clouds and rain).

'Theravada Buddhists speak of the Buddha's life and of the teaching he left, without the three-body scheme': confirm fair; some Pali texts use dhammakaya (e.g. DN 27) and a Keeper may want that named.
Source for the three-body scheme given as the Mahayanasutralamkara; a Keeper may prefer another text (e.g. the Suvarnaprabhasa).

Editor: 'this body, which is going to rot' changed to 'this foul body' (closer to SN 22.87's putikaya); 'the life this path followed last year' changed to 'in its stories' (the life story was told in year one, not last year). Vakkali was also used on days 351 and 1042; kept here because the angle (the three bodies) is new.
